title: Arithmetic Progression
prerequisites: Ability to identify patterns in a sequence of numbers.
Comfort with substituting into a formula.
Skill in solving linear and quadratic equations.

topics.title: Arithmetic Progression and the nth Term
topics.quick_summary: An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which each term differs from the previous one by a fixed common difference d, and its nth term is a + (n − 1)d.
topics.real_life: A salary rising by a fixed increment each year, or the seats increasing row by row in an auditorium, are arithmetic progressions.

detailed.definition: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers in which each term, except the first, is obtained by adding a fixed number d, the common difference, to the preceding term.
detailed.key_idea: The coefficient of d is (n − 1), not n, because the first term needs no addition at all. This off-by-one is the most frequent source of error in the whole chapter.
detailed.working_principle: To check whether a sequence is an AP, verify that a₂ − a₁ = a₃ − a₂ = a₄ − a₃. A single equal difference is not enough.
applications: The nth term from the end of an AP with l as the last term is l − (n − 1)d.
Three terms in AP are conveniently taken as a − d, a, a + d.
A negative d gives a decreasing AP.

points: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference.
d = aₙ − aₙ₋₁, and must be the same throughout.
The nth term from the end = l − (n − 1)d.
For three terms in AP, take a − d, a, a + d to simplify algebra.
d > 0 gives an increasing AP; d < 0 a decreasing one.
mistakes: Using a + nd instead of a + (n − 1)d.
Checking only one pair of consecutive terms before declaring a sequence an AP.
topics.memory_hook: 'First term needs no step, so multiply d by (n − 1), never n.'
topics.advanced: An AP is a linear function of n, so its graph is a set of collinear points. This is why the sum formula is quadratic in n — summing a linear function always gives a quadratic.

formulas.name: nth Term of an AP
formulas.variables: a = first term, d = common difference, n = term number.
formulas.when_to_use: To find any term, or to find n when a particular term is given.
formulas.common_mistakes: Using n instead of (n − 1) as the multiplier of d.
formulas.shortcut: If n comes out as a non-integer, that value is not a term of the AP.

topics.title: Sum of n Terms of an AP
topics.quick_summary: The sum of the first n terms of an AP is Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d], which equals (n/2)(a + l) when the last term is known.
topics.real_life: Total savings over ten years with a fixed annual increase is the sum of an AP — no need to add the ten amounts one by one.

detailed.definition: Sₙ denotes the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression. It is given by Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d] or equivalently (n/2)(a + l), where l is the last term.
detailed.key_idea: The second form is quicker whenever the last term is known, because it avoids computing d altogether. Choosing the right form halves the work.
detailed.working_principle: The formula comes from pairing the first and last terms, the second and second-last, and so on. Each pair sums to a + l, and there are n/2 such pairs.
applications: aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ recovers a term from the sums.
Sum of the first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2.
Sum of the first n odd numbers = n².

points: Sₙ = (n/2)(a + l) when the last term l is known.
Sum of the first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2.
If Sₙ is quadratic in n, the sequence is an AP.
mistakes: Using (n/2)(a + l) when l is not the nth term.
Forgetting the factor n/2 outside the bracket.
Solving a quadratic in n and keeping a negative or fractional value.
topics.memory_hook: 'Half the number of terms, times first plus last' — Gauss's schoolboy trick.
topics.advanced: Gauss reportedly summed 1 to 100 in seconds by pairing 1+100, 2+99, and so on. The general formula is nothing more than that pairing written in symbols.

formulas.name: Sum of n Terms of an AP
formulas.variables: n = number of terms, a = first term, d = common difference, l = last term.
formulas.when_to_use: To find a total, or to find n given the sum.
formulas.common_mistakes: Mixing the two forms and using both d and l in the same expression.
formulas.shortcut: Use (n/2)(a + l) whenever the last term is given.
